study.title: Lyapunov-controlled thermalization: an exact real-time example

cover.headline: A quantum system can **look perfectly thermal** but still hide exact memory of where it started.

slides.title: The team modeled a Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev quench protocol in the large-N, large-q limit.
slides.body:
They solved the exact real-time evolution of a unitary interacting many-body system after an energy quench. The model involves fermion correlators that appear to satisfy the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger relation once the drive stops, a hallmark of thermal equilibrium.

Then they applied a second quench back to the initial Hamiltonian to test whether the system had truly thermalized or retained hidden information about its initial state.

slides.title: All post-quench fermion correlators were exactly thermal, yet the second quench revealed hidden memory.
slides.body:
Despite the system appearing to satisfy every test for equilibrium, correlators connecting to times before the first quench exposed an extensive nonequilibrium witness. The memory persisted even though the standard thermal signature was perfect.

In this early paper, the team reports that the decay rate of this hidden memory matched the Lyapunov exponent, meaning the system only becomes effectively indistinguishable from a true Gibbs state at a rate set by that exponent.

slides.title: The Lyapunov exponent sets the timescale for a quantum system to forget its past.
slides.body:
In this early paper, the team reports that passing standard thermal tests after a quench is not sufficient evidence of equilibrium. The hidden correlators act as a witness to nonequilibrium structure that standard measurements miss entirely.

Because the large-N, large-q limit allows exact analytical solutions, the setup offers a rare window into how thermalization unfolds in real time in a chaotic interacting system.

caveats: This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed, so no independent expert has checked the work yet.
The analysis applies to a specific model in a mathematical limit, not to experiments with real materials or devices.

caption: A quantum many-body system can satisfy every standard test for thermal equilibrium and still retain an exact memory of its initial state. In this early paper, researchers modeled a Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev quench protocol in the large-N, large-q limit and found that post-quench fermion correlators looked perfectly thermal. But a second quench revealed hidden correlators encoding the system's past, decaying at a rate set by the Lyapunov exponent. The model is theoretical and applies in a specific mathematical limit.
